sketches.title: Tiny Trouble: Warning Labels for Harmless Things
sketches.premise: I deal an ordinary thing, and both of us write a warning label that makes it sound like a tiny menace. The Judge checks whether each label still truthfully fits the thing; then points reward the label that goes furthest without breaking that truth. Prepare to make a spoon sound suspicious.
sketches.criterion: The warning must describe a possible, genuine feature, use, effect, or risk of the dealt thing, without claiming it is inherently dangerous.
sketches.move_shape: Write one warning-label headline and one short supporting line, both about the card; for a spoon: “MAY CAUSE UNEXPECTED REFLECTIONS — Especially when pointed at your face during pudding negotiations.”

sketches.title: Fine Print Fiasco
sketches.premise: I deal a harmless everyday thing, and each of us writes the strangest fine-print rule that could honestly belong with it. The Judge awards points for stretching the truth into a clever restriction, while the other player guesses which rule the House invented. Read carefully; the loophole is wearing a tiny hat.
sketches.criterion: The rule must remain a plausible instruction or condition for using, carrying, storing, or encountering the dealt thing.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence of mock fine print beginning with “By using this…” or “Do not…”; for a backpack: “By using this backpack, you agree that one snack may be crushed beyond recognition.”

sketches.title: Side-Effect Society
sketches.premise: I deal a harmless thing, and both players announce a ridiculous-sounding side effect that can still genuinely happen when someone uses it. The Judge scores the most surprising consequence that keeps its feet on the ground. The medicine cabinet is not involved, despite the title.
sketches.criterion: The side effect must be a real or reasonably possible consequence of using, handling, seeing, hearing, or being near the card.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence in the form “May cause…”; for a whistle: “May cause every nearby dog to join the conversation.”

sketches.title: Not For Everyone
sketches.premise: I deal an ordinary object, and each of us writes a playful exclusion notice naming who should not use it and why. The Judge rewards a specific, unexpected restriction that remains fair and true, not a random insult. Even a sock has standards.
sketches.criterion: The notice must identify a real situation, person, condition, or purpose for which the card is unsuitable or inappropriate.
sketches.move_shape: Write one “Not recommended for…” notice with a reason; for a ladder: “Not recommended for people hoping to reach the top shelf while carrying three pizzas.”

sketches.title: Handle With Care-ish
sketches.premise: I deal a harmless thing, and both players write a caution that makes ordinary handling sound like a delicate operation. The Judge gives points for useful truth dressed in dramatic language, with no invented danger required. Please remain calm around the paperclip.
sketches.criterion: The caution must preserve a genuine way the card can be mishandled, damaged, inconvenient, or unexpectedly effective.
sketches.move_shape: Write one caution beginning “Handle with care when…”; for a balloon: “Handle with care when near cats, birthday candles, or anyone who says, ‘Watch this.’”

sketches.title: Officially Suspicious
sketches.premise: I deal a harmless thing, and each player gives it a mock official warning classification based on something it really does, resembles, or is used for. The Judge scores the classification that sounds most alarmingly official while staying accurate. Your first suspect is a banana.
sketches.criterion: The classification must truthfully connect the card to a real appearance, behavior, use, sound, or association without declaring a false danger.
sketches.move_shape: Write a stamped-looking classification and a reason; for a banana: “CLASS B: SLIPPERY CURVED OBJECT — Handle carefully during dramatic entrances.”
